    Home/Learn/Is BPC-157 legal in the US? What the FDA decided

    Is BPC-157 legal? What the FDA says in 2026.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    Not approved: FDA advisory committee reviewed it for compounding on 23 Jul 2026; FDA proposed not to allow it.1

    What is BPC-157?

    BPC-157 is a lab-made peptide, a short chain of amino acids. Online shops sell it as a "healing peptide", mostly as a powder in a vial that is meant to be mixed and injected. You will also see it in capsules and nasal sprays.

    The studies behind it are in animals and in cells. We found no large trials in people, and the FDA says it found no, or only limited, information on its safety in people for the ways it was proposed to be used.2

    Is BPC-157 FDA approved?

    No. There is no FDA-approved medicine that contains BPC-157, for any use. An approved medicine is one whose maker sent the FDA its trial data and the FDA found that the benefits outweigh the known risks for the people it is meant for.3 Nobody has done that for BPC-157.

    The FDA's page on substances that may be risky in pharmacy-made medicines lists BPC-157 among those whose nomination for pharmacy compounding was withdrawn. It says BPC-157 made by a pharmacy may set off an immune reaction when given some ways, may be hard to make free of unwanted peptide fragments, and has little or no safety information behind it.2

    What did the FDA review in July 2026?

    On 23 and 24 July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, a panel of outside experts, reviewed BPC-157 together with TB-500, MOTS-c and epitalon. The question was whether pharmacies may use these substances to make medicines for patients on a prescription. The FDA proposed not to allow it.1

    A committee advises; the FDA decides. A proposal is a step, not the last word. We keep the status on our Is it legal today? table and change this page when the FDA publishes what it decided.

    Is BPC-157 the same as TB-500?

    No. TB-500 is a lab-made copy of part of a natural repair protein, and shops often sell it next to BPC-157 or in the same blend. It went through the same July 2026 review and got the same proposal: not approved, and the FDA proposed not to let pharmacies use it.1

    A blend of the two is not a tested product either. Nobody has studied the mix in people, and a lab report for a blend rarely says how much of each peptide is in the vial.

    What does "research use only" mean?

    "Research use only" and "not for human use" are words the shop puts on its own label. They do not mean that anyone approved the product, and they tell you nothing about what is in the vial or how clean it is.

    The label also means there is no dose on the box and no instructions from a doctor or pharmacist. We do not give doses either, and we never link to these shops.

    What are research-use shops doing?

    They keep selling it, in vials of different sizes and in blends with other peptides.

    A lab report is a start, not proof. It covers one batch, tested once, and it is only worth something if a lab outside the shop did the test. Our guide on how to read a peptide COA shows what to look for.

    How do we check the shops that sell it?

    For every shop we hold the same five checks: Lab reports, No FDA letter, Company found, Legal pages and Fresh prices. Each one is a yes or no that we can show the source for, and we add them up to a score out of five.

    On our recovery page, the BPC-157 row has a "Prices at" button with the number of shops. It opens a window with the shops, each with its price per mg, its five checks and six facts: a COA for that listing, FDA warning letters, the registered company, whether the shop is active, when we first saw it and when we last checked the price.

    These checks are facts we hold about the shop. They are not a safety or quality grade, and a shop with five of five is still selling a product that is not approved.
